money-market-s1.title: A money market after a shift

money-market-s2.title: A recession in an invented economy
money-market-s2.text: Real GDP in the invented country of Venna falls sharply in a recession, while the price level barely changes. Households and firms buy fewer goods and services. Venna's central bank keeps the money supply where it was.

items.q: The graph shows money demand shifting from MD1 to MD2. Which event could have caused this shift?
options: A rise in the nominal interest rate
A rise in the price level
A rise in the money supply
Wider use of payment cards and phone apps

why.correct: Money demand shifts with the price level, real GDP and payment technology; the interest rate moves along it.
options: A change in the interest rate moves along money demand; it does not shift it.
Right: higher prices mean people need more money for the same purchases, so MD shifts right.
That would shift the vertical MS curve, not MD.
Easier payments let people hold less money, which shifts MD left.

items.q: In the graph, what happens to the equilibrium nominal interest rate?
options: It falls, because more money is demanded
It stays the same, because the money supply is fixed
It rises, from i1 to i2
It rises at first, then returns to i1

why.correct: With a vertical money supply, a rightward shift of money demand raises the nominal interest rate and leaves the quantity of money unchanged.
options: More money demanded with a fixed supply pushes the rate up, not down.
The fixed supply is why the rate must rise to balance the larger demand.
Right: MD2 crosses the vertical MS at a higher nominal interest rate.
With MS unchanged, the new equilibrium stays at the higher rate.

items.q: As the economy moves to the new equilibrium in the graph, what happens to the prices of existing bonds?
options: They fall, as people sell bonds to get money
They rise, as people buy bonds
They do not change, since bonds are not money
They rise, because interest rates rise

why.correct: Bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions; selling bonds to raise money pushes bond prices down.
options: Right: to hold more money, people sell bonds, which lowers bond prices and raises interest rates.
People want more money, so they sell bonds rather than buy them.
Bonds are how people adjust their money holdings, so their prices move.
Bond prices move opposite to interest rates: the rate rises, so bond prices fall.

items.q: In the graph, what happens to the quantity of money in the new equilibrium?
options: It rises, because demand rose
It stays the same
It falls, because the interest rate rose
It rises, then falls back

why.correct: A shift of money demand along a vertical money supply changes the interest rate, not the quantity of money.
options: The money supply is vertical: the central bank fixes the quantity, so it does not rise.
Right: the vertical MS fixes the quantity; only the interest rate changes.
The quantity is set by the vertical MS and does not move with the rate.
The quantity of money stays where MS is throughout.

items.q: On the money market graph, show the effect of Venna's recession and mark the new equilibrium.

why.correct: Lower real GDP means fewer transactions, so people need less money: money demand shifts left, and with a fixed money supply the nominal interest rate falls.

slips.MS: The scenario says the central bank keeps the money supply where it was. Lower income changes how much money people want to hold: money demand.

items.q: Why does the recession change the demand for money in Venna?
options: People buy fewer goods, so they need less money for transactions
Interest rates fall, so people want more money
The central bank prints less money
Prices rise, so people need more money

why.correct: The transaction demand for money depends on nominal GDP: fewer purchases mean less money is needed.
options: Right: the transaction demand for money falls with real GDP.
That is a movement along money demand, which follows from the shift; it is not the cause.
The scenario says the money supply is unchanged.
The scenario says the price level barely changes.

items.q: What happens to the prices of existing bonds in Venna?
options: They fall, because people need less money
They rise, as the nominal interest rate falls
They are unchanged, since the money supply is fixed
They fall, as the nominal interest rate falls

why.correct: A fall in money demand lowers the nominal interest rate, and lower interest rates mean higher prices for existing bonds.
options: With less money needed, people use the extra to buy bonds, which raises bond prices.
Right: people put money they no longer need into bonds, so bond prices rise and rates fall.
The fixed supply is why the interest rate, and bond prices, must change.
Bond prices move opposite to interest rates: a lower rate means higher bond prices.

items.q: Suppose Venna's price level had also fallen during the recession. How would that change your answer about money demand?
options: Money demand would fall by more
Money demand would rise instead
Money demand would not change
Money supply would shift left instead

why.correct: Money demand depends on nominal GDP, the price level times real GDP; a fall in either shifts it left.
options: Right: lower prices and lower real output both mean less money is needed for purchases.
Lower prices mean each purchase takes less money, so demand falls further, not rises.
Both the price level and real GDP shift money demand.
The price level shifts money demand; the money supply is set by the central bank.

items.q: Label the axes and the curves of the money market graph.

why.correct: The money market has the nominal interest rate on the vertical axis and the quantity of money on the horizontal axis, with downward-sloping money demand (MD) and vertical money supply (MS).

items.q: With limited reserves, the central bank increases the money supply. Shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

why.correct: More money shifts the vertical money supply right; people hold the extra money only at a lower nominal interest rate.

key.because: an increase in the money supply

slips.MD: The central bank changed how much money exists, which is the money supply, not how much people want to hold.

items.q: Mark point A on the money demand curve at a nominal interest rate above the equilibrium rate.

why.correct: Along MD, a higher nominal interest rate means a smaller quantity of money demanded, so A sits up and to the left of the equilibrium.

items.q: Why does the money demand curve slope down?
options: A higher price level means people need less money
The nominal interest rate is the opportunity cost of holding money
The central bank supplies less money at high rates
Banks lend more when interest rates rise

why.correct: Money pays little or no interest, so the interest given up on bonds is the cost of holding it: higher rates, less money demanded.
options: A higher price level shifts money demand right; it does not explain the slope.
Right: when bonds pay more, holding cash costs more, so people hold less of it.
The money supply is vertical; the slope of demand comes from households' choices.
That is about lending, not about how much money people choose to hold.

items.q: What goes on the vertical axis of the money market graph?
options: The real interest rate
The price level
The nominal interest rate
The quantity of money

why.correct: Money market: nominal interest rate (vertical) and quantity of money (horizontal). Writing "real" loses the graph point.
options: The real rate goes on a different graph later in this unit. The money market uses the nominal rate.
The price level goes on the AD-AS graph.
Right: the opportunity cost of holding money is the nominal rate.
The quantity of money is on the horizontal axis.

items.q: In the money market, the nominal interest rate is above equilibrium. How does the market move back to equilibrium?
options: People hold more money than they want, buy bonds, and the rate falls
People want more money, sell bonds, and the rate rises
The central bank lowers the money supply until the rate matches
People hold more money than they want, sell bonds, and the rate rises

why.correct: A surplus of money leads people to buy bonds: bond prices rise and interest rates fall until people want to hold the money that exists.
options: Right: buying bonds raises bond prices, which lowers interest rates.
Above equilibrium people want less money than exists, not more.
The market adjusts through bond buying; the supply does not have to change.
With surplus money, people buy bonds, which lowers the rate.

items.q: Which of these shift the money demand curve to the right? Select all that apply.
options: A rise in the price level
A rise in real GDP
A rise in the nominal interest rate
Wider use of payment cards and phone apps

why.correct: Money demand shifts right with nominal GDP (the price level or real output); the nominal interest rate moves along it.
options: Right: each purchase takes more money.
Right: more transactions need more money.
A rate change is a movement along money demand, not a shift.
Easier payments reduce how much money people hold, a shift to the left.

items.q: Put the links in order, from a rise in the price level to bond prices.
options: The price level rises
People need more money for the same purchases, so money demand shifts right
People sell bonds to get money
Bond prices fall and the nominal interest rate rises

why.correct: Each link causes the next: more money demanded, bonds sold, bond prices down, the interest rate up.

items.q: Make it specific: explain how a rise in the price level affects the nominal interest rate when the money supply does not change.

why.correct: A higher price level raises money demand; with a fixed money supply the nominal interest rate rises (and bond prices fall).

specific.frame: The price level rises, so money demand shifts ___; with a vertical money supply the nominal interest rate ___, and the prices of existing bonds ___.
specific.model: The price level rises, so people need more money for the same purchases and money demand shifts right; because the money supply is fixed, the nominal interest rate increases and the prices of existing bonds decrease.

direction.label: Money demand shifts
options: right
left

why.1: Higher prices mean more money is needed for each purchase, so demand rises.

rate.label: The nominal interest rate
options: rises
falls

why.1: More demand for a fixed supply raises the price of holding money, the interest rate.

price.label: Bond prices
options: fall
rise

why.1: Bond prices move opposite to interest rates.

items.q: Why is the money supply drawn as a vertical line on the money market graph?
options: People want the same amount of money at any interest rate
Banks hold more reserves when interest rates rise
The central bank sets the quantity of money, whatever the interest rate
The quantity of money grows as interest rates rise

why.correct: In the money market model the central bank fixes the quantity of money, so the money supply curve is vertical.
options: That would describe money demand, which slopes down.
The graph treats the quantity of money as set by the central bank, not by rates.
Right: the quantity does not respond to the rate, so supply is vertical.
That would be an upward-sloping supply curve, not a vertical one.
